title: Pierogi
subtitle: Polish dumplings filled with potato and cheese
excerpt: The most loved Polish dumpling: simple unleavened dough wrapped around a filling of mashed potato and cottage cheese, boiled until cooked through, then finished in butter until lightly golden. Served with soured cream and fried onions.

recipe.sourceNotes: Pierogi (singular pieróg) are filled dumplings that are the single most iconic dish of Polish cuisine, eaten in households across Poland at every meal of the day and on every occasion. The dough is simple: wheat flour, soured cream, and egg. The fillings are numerous: ruskie (potato and white cheese, the most popular), kapusta i grzyby (sauerkraut and mushroom, the Christmas Eve version), meat, and sweet versions filled with fruit. Pierogi ruskie, the potato-cheese filling, is the canonical everyday version, despite the misleading name (ruskie refers to the historical region of Ruthenia, not Russia). In Poland, boiled pierogi are often finished in a pan with butter and onions to give them a lightly golden surface, which adds flavour and texture.

content.text: The dough must be soft and elastic, not sticky. Cover it and rest for 30 minutes; this rest makes it much easier to roll thinly. Seal the edges firmly by pressing with your fingertips and then crimping with a fork; any gap will let the filling escape during boiling. Cook in batches and do not overcrowd the pot or they will stick together.

content.text: Make the dough: mix the flour, egg, soured cream, and 0.5 teaspoon of salt to a soft dough. Knead for 5 minutes until smooth. Wrap and rest for 30 minutes at room temperature. Make the filling: fry the diced onion in a little butter until golden. Mix with the mashed potato, cottage cheese, and cheddar. Season with salt and pepper. Cool completely.

Roll the dough on a floured surface to about 2 mm thick. Cut circles of about 8 cm with a glass or cutter. Place a heaped teaspoon of filling in the centre of each circle. Fold the dough over into a half-moon and press the edges firmly together. Crimp with a fork. Place on a floured tray.

Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil. Cook the pierogi in batches for 3 to 4 minutes until they float and the dough is cooked through. Remove with a slotted spoon. Melt the butter in a large frying pan over medium heat. Fry the sliced onion until golden. Add the boiled pierogi and fry for 2 minutes per side until lightly golden. Serve with soured cream.
